    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that air France delivered one of the best business class flights I have taken in years on my journey from Paris to New York.
    • I shared my first impressions of this flight earlier, calling it the best business class experience in Europe.
    • Sources indicate that I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that air France delivered one of the best business class flights I have taken in years on my journey from Paris to New York. The new A350-900 cabin is excellent, but what impressed me most was how well everything came together, from the comfortable seat to the delicious dinner, gracious service, and fast Starlink Wi-Fi.

    I shared my first impressions of this flight earlier, calling it the best business class experience in Europe. Having had more time to reflect on it, I stand by that assessment…this flight left very little room for improvement.

    Sources indicate that I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer. Flying Blue came through with a last-minute business class award from Basel to Paris to Upcoming York for 60,000 miles plus €453 in taxes and fees. The timing worked perfectly and I booked this about 36-hour before departure, so saver space can certainly open up via FlyingBlue.

    This was a so-called “reverse redeye,” leaving Europe late in the evening and arriving in the United States even later that same evening. That suited my plans very well, particularly because I had an overnight drive to Pittsburgh ahead of me after landing.

    My journey began in Basel with an Air France Hop! flight to Paris. I had time to visit the lounge before my connection and enjoyed a meal there, though I deliberately left room for dinner onboard.

    Stepping onboard, I found my seat in 6L. Though approaching 8:00 pm, it was still very light outside.

    It has been revealed that I first reviewed Air France A350 business class in 2020, flying from Paris to Toronto. I enjoyed that flight very much, but the newer business class cabin represents a substantial improvement.

    Sources indicate that the business class cabin has 48 seats spread over a front and rear cabin. These seats are based on the Stelia Opera platform and are arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration, with every passenger having direct aisle access and a sliding door to provide additional privacy.

    Far more important the gimmicky door was the room for your feet, which I found plentiful. Legroom is 43 inches when the seat is the upright position and it transforms into a bed that is 79 inches long. Seats are 21 inches wide.

    There are no personal art vents, but thankfully the cabin was kept very chilly. I also loved the window darkening feature, where the window tinting could be adjusted simply by sliding your finger left or right.

    According to recent reports, I found this suite spacious and comfortable whether sitting upright, reclining, or lying down. The cabin looks so sharp. I particularly love the illuminated winged seahorse at each seat…a small detail, but one that gives the cabin an unmistakable Air France identity.

    There was plenty of personal storage, and the wireless charging worked well, though there was also USB-C and universal A/C power.

    After dinner, I converted my seat into a bed and slept for about four hours.

    The Sofitel-branded bedding (duvet, mattress pad, pillow) was excellent, and I found the seat very comfortable for sleeping.

    This is one of my favorite business class seats.

    It has been revealed that air France provided a very attractive amenity kit with an embossed seahorse on the bag. It was lined with red and the contents included:.

    The catering was a highlight of this flight. I had eaten in the lounge, but was very glad I saved room for dinner.

    Before takeoff, flight attendants offered Champagne and a warm towel, along with the familiar Gavottes savory biscuits.

    The full menu (every menu item and ingredient is French except for Coca-Cola):.

    Dinner began with an appetizer of pea, lemon, and basil cream accompanied by smoked salmon fillet and raspberry and grapefruit jelly.

    A side salad accompanied the starter, though I saved mine until after the main course, as the French do. The bread was delicious.

    I also tried the Quintessence cocktail, an Air France variation on a Negroni. It combined La Quintinye royal red vermouth, bitter Chambéry liqueur, a hint of fig, and ABK6 VSOP Cognac. I enjoyed it very much. It was not nearly as strong as a traditional Negroni, which suited me just fine on this flight.

    For my main course, I chose veal with a creamy morel mushroom sauce, spelt risotto, and peas.

    Sources indicate that admittedly, the presentation was not going to win any awards…yes, it looked like vomit. But it tasted delicious and I would happily order it again. I enjoyed a delicious glass of Chateau D’Arsac wine, which was so good.

    Industry observers note that A cheese course followed, then dessert. I enjoyed both ice cream and a crispy hazelnut tart, accompanied by hot chocolate.

    This was a substantial supper and a very satisfying one.

    About an hour before landing, flight attendants served a light meal of shrimp with a pickled cucumber salad.

    According to recent reports, it was excellent and just the right amount of food after the large dinner. I had two espressos with it, which helped prepare me for the late night ahead.

    The entertainment system included a tail camera, which I particularly enjoyed during our departure from Paris (though not the fire that seemed to be burning near CDG). It was a gorgeous evening, and watching the aircraft leave Charles de Gaulle was a lovely way to begin the flight.

    I did not watch any movies or TV on this flight, but there was large selection of movies, TV shows, games, and music.

    Noise-cancelling headphones were provided, though you can also connect your own Bluetooth device.

    Sources indicate that fast, free Starlink internet was available onboard. The connection worked from gate to gate and felt much like using the internet on the ground. I did not have any essential work to complete on this flight, but I appreciated being able to connect onboard. Starlink increasingly influences which flights I book. Air France already gives me plenty of reasons to choose it, but reliable internet makes the proposition even more attractive, especially for a daytime westbound journey when I might otherwise spend several hours working.

    The Air France A350 has three lavatories in business class: one I the front (though typically reserved for crew use) and two in between the front and rear cabin.

    According to recent reports, service was warm and attentive throughout the flight. I was even addressed by surname.

    Recent findings suggest that I have heard plenty of complaints over the years about service on Air France, but my own experiences have been very positive. This crew continued that pattern and the great service complemented the rest of the experience. I enjoyed a delicious meal, slept comfortably, and felt well cared for throughout the journey.

    Recent findings suggest that the new seat deserves attention, but a cabin can only do so much without a good crew in terms of leaving a lasting positive impression. On this flight, Air France delivered both.

    Sources indicate that we landed on time at JFK, and I promptly cleared immigration using Global Entry. The late arrival had been part of the appeal when booking, and the flight delivered exactly what I had hoped for: an enjoyable evening onboard, a few hours of rest, and an on-time arrival in Fresh York.

    Then it was time to collect a rental car and begin my overnight drive to Pittsburgh….

    This was a tremendous flight on Air France…I have no complaints at all about anything.

    I liked the older A350 business class product when I flew it in 2020, but the newer seat is a considerable improvement. Pair that with excellent bedding, delicious food, and a gracious crew, then add Starlink, and I struggle to identify much that I would change. Cappuccinos maybe that are not powdered?

    The lack of individual air vents remains a drawback, though the comfortable cabin temperature thankfully meant it did not interfere with my sleep on this flight.

    According to recent reports, air France reminded me how enjoyable a transatlantic business class flight can be when the airline gets the details right. I would happily book this product again and would go out of my way to find it.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A subsidiary of China Southern Airlines has agreed to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, Reuters reported Tuesday.
    • The airplanes, which have a total list price of $7.4 billion, will be used by Xiamen Airlines, which is based in Fujian.
    • In a recent development, the deal is Boeing’s largest with a Chinese operator in nearly a decade.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A subsidiary of China Southern Airlines has agreed to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, Reuters reported Tuesday.

    The airplanes, which have a total list price of $7.4 billion, will be used by Xiamen Airlines, which is based in Fujian. Deliveries are expected from 2031 to 2034.

    In a recent development, the deal is Boeing’s largest with a Chinese operator in nearly a decade. The country largely shifted toward Airbus aircraft as relations with the U.S. frayed.

    According to recent reports, president Donald Trump hoped to reverse that trend during his state visit to China in May. Trump discussed a potential purchase directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and even brought along Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg for the summit. Ultimately, Beijing agreed to buy 200 aircraft from Boeing, fewer than analysts expected, but still notable considering Boeing’s drought in the country.

    Trump said earlier this week that he thinks China will buy 250 more aircraft from Boeing. He did not provide details or say where that information came from.

    China Southern noted the latest aircraft will help Xiamen expand after it relocates to the new Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport. The facility will replace Xiamen Gaoqi International Airport as Xiamen’s main gateway.

    #122828. A Real-Life Santa’s Workshop: How Macy’s Parade Studio Works All Year to Prep for Thanksgiving Day Magic

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2365 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    A Real-Life Santa’s Workshop: How Macy’s Parade Studio Works All Year to Prep for Thanksgiving Day Magic

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Santa’s workshop just might be inside a rather plain red-and-black brick building in northern Fresh Jersey.
    • This year, the festivities are grander than ever, as the team has toiled for two years in preparation for a major milestone: the parade’s 100th edition.
    • A snapshot of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from 1940.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Santa’s workshop just might be inside a rather plain red-and-black brick building in northern Fresh Jersey. Sitting about 10 miles northwest of Midtown Manhattan in Moonachie’s industrial park district, the 72,000-square-foot warehouse is home to Macy’s Parade Studio, where 60 designers, carpenters, welders, seamstresses, and other artisans chip away year-round to prepare for one morning a year: the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

    This year, the festivities are grander than ever, as the team has toiled for two years in preparation for a major milestone: the parade’s 100th edition. Instead of the normal 50 to 60 inflatables, there will be nearly 100. The usual 500 fresh costumes will be upped to 1,000, while more than 11,000 volunteers will be a part of the milestone event.

    A snapshot of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from 1940.

    Industry observers note that it’s a massive endeavor for a tradition that started as a two-block-long procession of Central Park Zoo animals, a handful of bands, and Santa, all traveling six miles from Harlem to the department store’s flagship in Herald Square at 34th and Broadway in 1924 (it was suspended for three years during World War II from 1942 to 1944). The parade led to the unveiling of Macy’s window displays with puppets by marionette artist Tony Sarg to kick off the holiday—and retail—season.

    According to recent reports, “It started as a bunch of Macy's immigrant coworkers coming together to create a party like they had in their home countries,” Brendan Kennedy, director of creative production, tells me during a visit in late September. But soon, the animals were deemed to be “too scary” for children. Three years later, the balloons debuted, the work of Sarg, who he calls “one of the godfathers of puppetry” and “our Walt Disney.” His genius idea: flip marionettes upside down to become high-flying balloons on strings, creating the iconic tradition we know today.

    Taking a peek at the concept art hanging inside the Macy's workshop.

    According to recent reports, wandering through the facility is like making your way through a pop culture fun house. A pair of Minions hang from the rafters, mingling with Pokémon’s Pikachu and Goofy, who is stuck in a wreath. A Planter’s Peanut Ferris wheel spins in the center, while models of the parade’s own famous characters, Tom Turkey, Blue Hippopotamus, and the fishy pair Rainbow and Greybow Trout, sit out to dry in front of shelves lined with paint buckets of every hue.

    It has been revealed that “This is like our own Hollywood lot,” Kennedy says. Indeed, there’s the distinct feel of a soundstage paired with the wildest arts and crafts studio you've ever seen, all together feeling like something out of Willy Wonka’s dreams. Before making its home here in 2011, the Parade Studio was located inside the old Tootsie Roll factory in Hoboken, Upcoming Jersey, for decades.

    Despite the holiday joy bursting from every seam, parade preparation is serious business. Every single element is handcrafted and hand-painted. "Generally it all starts with a napkin sketch,” Kennedy explains of the initial rough drawing. “It goes into full modeling in 3-D, and then engineering, where we have to figure out how to get this thing into the real world.”.

    It has been revealed that but year after year, like the true elves of the holiday season they are, they pull it off—testing every float and balloon for any and every possible weather condition—so that on Thanksgiving morning, the 3.5 million lining the Manhattan route as well as the nearly 35 million watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade at home (airing on NBC and Peacock from 8:30 a.m. to noon) can just sit back and revel in the delights of the season.

    “What makes the parade so special is that it is an event that has been produced by colleagues since it began in 1924, and it continues to be Macy Studios colleagues' gift to Upcoming York City and gift to people who are tuning in around the country to watch on television,” Macy’s director of production operations Kathleen Wright tells Traveler.

    Below, we peek behind the scenes of the Macy’s Parade Studio as the team prepares for the 100th parade, and how they plan to honor the traditions of the last century.

    Some of the 3-D printed models that serve as the blueprints for the parade's iconic floats.

    Sources indicate that the larger-than-life magic of the parade starts on the smallest scale. In the Studio’s 3-D print room, nearly a dozen machines hum away, creating miniature models—the first step in conceiving how to build each float. But that’s not the only tool used. Recently, engineers and sculptors have turned to augmented reality goggles, not just to picture the elements, but even wearing them while sculpting to make sure they get details right in a 3-D space.

    The day I visit, the team is problem-solving on the fresh Purina Dog Chow Salute to Service Dogs float, which features three oversized dog puppets.

    An array of the painted models inside the studio.

    In a recent development, “When floats come to life through some sort of animation is when it’s at its peak,” Kennedy indicates. While animatronics could provide the movements, they would lack the human touch. “With a puppet, I can look directly at you, give you a little show, and then pan to the next person. You get a lot more energy and excitement. There’s a long history of puppetry in the parade, so we made a concerted effort to include it.”.

    Sources indicate that the team works through solutions for the best way to have a puppeteer lie below the float bed, controlling the motions from below while positioned with body pillows that still allow them to see the parade-goers through a scrim. They consider using delivery truck slats to increase the height of the float so the puppeteer can remain comfortable and still operate the puppet.

    In a recent development, mr. Peanut is the historic parade's oldest character.

    It has been revealed that in another section, another upcoming float is going for a test spin. Planters’ Mr. Peanut Power Plant will celebrate the parade’s oldest character, with peanut-shaped confetti erupting through his top hat, as well as a rotating Ferris wheel showcasing his evolution from 1916, starting with the napkin sketch created by a 13-year-old boy from Virginia.

    According to recent reports, also on the floor is a puppet of the original character Mr. Inspector, a stern-looking comic book character with a top hat and magnifying glass, who first appeared as a balloon in the 1929 parade. This version of the character was taken out of the archives and freshened up in order to be part of Macy’s own Tony Sarg’s Amazing Marionettes float.

    “Everything has to be refurbished,” Kennedy states. “These are Latest York City streets—it’s not like a perfect Narnia land. So they hit a bump, we have to work through it, or if it rains, we have to check for water damage.”.

    According to recent reports, while the methods are precise, the methodology is all about creativity and resourcefulness. Case in point: While working on the Wednesday Addams float in 2024, Tim Burton himself asked for more decay and rot. So a sculptor modified his glue gun to spray spider webs around the entire float. “It’s a good example of how anything can become a tool,” he says of making fiction come to life.

    Sources indicate that but there are some strict restrictions. Floats have to fold up to the size of a standard city bus in order to fit through the Lincoln Tunnel into Manhattan. The massive convoy travels in two nights before Thanksgiving. Once settled, the team reassembles every piece, some using cranes, as every float gets its final touches before the significant day.

    Peeking inside the planning of the parade's Mickey Mouse float.

    In a recent development, next, we step into the Balloon Studio, where again, everything starts with a 3-D model. After it’s approved, a larger form “white model,” roughly a few feet long, is generated (clay models were used in the past) and used to hand-draw lines that determine the shapes and sizes of each piece of balloon fabric that needs to be cut and how they’ll be melded together, much like sewing with a dress pattern.

    In a recent development, dangling from beams above is a display of white models of the past, with the monotone versions of Super Mario, Buzz Lightyear, Snoopy, and the Pillsbury Doughboy, among others. But today the focus is on the freshly-completed Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey Mouse, hanging from a little stand to mimic levitation. I count no less than nine pieces of fabric sketched out in pencil just for the nose—and about 18 for the front side of each ear.

    Artisans stitch together all the massive textiles that go onto the floats.

    At the next station, we see a pair of artisans doing seemingly mundane work stitching large swaths of fabric together with sewing machines. To a trained eye, though, the scene is actually chock full of proprietary Macy’s secrets. While rubber was used in the past, today the balloons are made of off-white secret material the makeup of which is closely guarded. The material is heat-sealed together using these Macy’s-designed machines with wheels that heat up to 410 degrees Fahrenheit. Then the material is painted using a formula that’s also—you guessed it—proprietary.

    Sources indicate that the secrets all come together as the completed balloons are first inflated indoors to make sure that the paint looks good and to check how it behaves with air. Some are inspected in the Studio while others that require more space are pumped up from the floor since it would float at the nearby Prudential Center. The balloons are inflated at various stages to ensure the air is filling up as intended.

    The big test came on November 7, when they hosted the annual Balloonfest at MetLife Stadium to see how the balloons behave in outdoor conditions, as well as give city agencies the chance to approve everything.

    Once that’s checked off, the night before the parade is the Balloon Inflation (which is open to the public; stay tuned for details here), when each character is blown up on the streets of the Upper West Side and prepped for its own turkey trot through Midtown. “They really are flying pieces of art,” Kennedy claims.

    A shimmering Christmas tree costume.

    A dress from the costume operations studio.

    While the floats and balloons may get the headlines, there would be no parade without the nearly 11,000 volunteers who help make the day happen, which is now 2.5-miles from the Upper West Side to Herald Square—and they all have to be dressed for the occasion. This year at least 1,500 more costumes are needed, but that doesn't intimidate costume director and associate producer Kimberly Montgomery, who’s been doing this for 27 years. “It’s gone so fast because it’s just been so darn fun,” she says of her tenure.

    Costumes follow after the design of the float, with the larger backdrop serving as the source of wardrobe inspiration.

    Every costume always begins in the same place. “We start with the design of the float and then riff off of that to tell a story with live people,” she explains. Just then, she catches a glimpse of a new design of a float with street signs and immediately starts brainstorming: “Maybe people on bikes will give it some texture and energy.” After all, she sees the floats as roving stages. "They're like mini Broadway shows.”.

    It has been revealed that when the very first 1924 parade arrived at Macy’s, it was met by employees dressed as clowns—and this year there will be 1,000 clowns throughout the parade, just a portion of the costume packets that she’s been working all year to assemble. And it's not just with what they'll wear. The late November weather is a major consideration as well. Costume kits also include ear and hand warmers, “the first two areas to get cold,” she claims. Most costumes are also made loose enough so that the paraders can layer up underneath.

    There are roughly 3,500 costumes produced for the balloon handler brigade.

    Balloon handlers get a different treatment. “Their costumes are a lot simpler because they have to pay attention to what they're doing,” she says. In fact, some balloons, like Buzz Lightyear, Sorcerer’s Mickey, and the Minion have nearly 100 people handling them. In total, about 3,500 of the costumes are for balloon handlers. “It’s serious business, so they get a coverall and a tabard that’s color coded with a picture of the character they’re holding.” She points out Toad the mushroom for Mario and an alien planet for Buzz Lightyear. And for the Minions, the team even has little cowboy hats.

    Of course there are odes to the past in the costumes too. Some historic costumes have been pulled out of the archives, like an intricate Broadway-quality Mother Goose dress. Others have been given new interpretations, like the original character Harold, who debuted in 1945 as a clown, but had stints as a baseball player (as he was seen in Miracle on 34th Street), fireman, and policeman. For this centennial, there will be 100 Harolds—25 of each iteration—as inflatable costumes (balloons aren’t the only ones that are blown up here!).

    Prepping for the significant day begin bright and early at 4:30 a.m.

    According to recent reports, with all this prep, dressing thousands of people then operates like clockwork, as they arrive around 4:30 a.m. at ballrooms around town in their street clothes and exit transformed. For 2.5 hours, shuttles transport them all to the parade start line.

    After all the pomp and circumstances are over, Montgomery turns to a latest phase of the process: Laundry. “All of this goes in giant piles of whites, darks, and colors. We’ve got to get it laundered and put back in size order.”.

    Sources indicate that and once everything is back in order, they start again on the following year’s parade. “No matter what holiday it is, we always have our finger on the pulse of Thanksgiving,” Wright says.

    Breaking: Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    Sources indicate that the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    In a recent development, hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    Sources indicate that that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an key part of it.”.

    “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    In a recent development, “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very manufacturer that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox mentioned in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    “We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson stated. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Recent findings suggest that myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She stated Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also said that Hawley’s newly introduced arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    Recent findings suggest that “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • “She got into college and was moving out of state, and it felt like this might be the last chance that I would possibly have to be with this girl,” Awaez remembered.
    • Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a middle-school field trip.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An incredible love story deserves an incredible wedding. Growing up in the Atlanta suburbs, Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a field trip in middle school, then became best friends as teenagers. It was toward the end of high school that their connection turned romantic.

    “She got into college and was moving out of state, and it felt like this might be the last chance that I would possibly have to be with this girl,” Awaez remembered. “We decided to see where things would take us.”.

    Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a middle-school field trip.

    The two grew up in the Atlanta area and got together toward the end of high school.

    The relationship took them into their twenties through to a proposal in July 2023: an elaborate scavenger hunt that Awaez staged around Chicago, where they lived briefly before turning to Atlanta. When plotting their wedding, they were sure they wanted something just as detailed and thoughtful, and immediately landed on a destination celebration. “We knew we didn’t want to have it in Atlanta, because we didn’t feel like we would be able to give our guests the kind of intentional experience we really wanted to,” indicates Falaknaz.

    Ahead, the couple explains how and why they chose to hold a Seville destination wedding in August 2025 for 160 guests, and discusses the (many!) venues they booked for their various events, the fun guest surprise they plotted, and loads of other sangria-soaked details.

    Hotel Alfonso XIII is an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for the Spanish king.

    The property and Sevilla in general are known for the Mudéjar-style architecture of Southern Spain.

    Industry observers note that falaknaz and Awaez were open to getting married anywhere, a wonderful but intimidating prospect. They scoured Pinterest and spoke to planners across the US. “We looked into Chicago, we looked into California, and at one point we looked into a cabin wedding in Montana,” the bride claims. “None of those really felt right until I came across some of the venues in Seville, Spain.”.

    It has been revealed that her major moment of connection was seeing the Hotel Alfonso XIII, an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for a king of Spain, who aimed to host esteemed international guests there. The scale and vibe of Seville itself—smaller than other European cities, but with an incredible history, stunning architecture, and loads to do—appealed as well. The couple reached out to several planners and booked a trip to visit the Alfonso and several other venues.

    Recent findings suggest that in person, the property was just as incredible as they’d hoped. “Hotel Alfonso was honestly a non-negotiable for me once we stayed there that very first trip,” says Awaez. “We were exposed to all the different ways we could utilize the hotel and make the most of it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that and given the hotel’s 150 rooms, the majority of their guest list could stay there, and did. “One of the major things we wanted from the wedding was everyone to be together. We loved the idea of it being almost a resort, where you’re constantly bumping into people from the wedding,” says Falaknaz.

    The couple chose event-planning firm Bodas del Sur because it had worked on South Asian weddings before.

    In a recent development, as they tried to narrow down the location for their wedding, the couple had a few dismaying calls with potential event firms. “We met with a lot of planners, and they had a lot of stipulations right off the bat. They weren't really open to hearing what we wanted out of our wedding,” Falaknaz states. They ultimately opted to work with Bodas del Sur, a Seville-based firm that specializes in destination weddings across Andalusia and gave them utter confidence in their ideas. “From our very first conversation, they just seemed like they were going to make what we wanted happen,” the bride continues. “Whatever we said, they ran with it, like, ‘Okay, these are all the ways we can make it happen.’ That was the most reassuring thing: that we felt heard.”.

    In addition to their vast experience with Seville venues and vendors, Bodas del Sur had also worked on South Asian weddings in the past, indicates the bride, “so it gave us a lot of confidence that they knew what they were doing.”.

    A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

    A key aspect of the typical South Asian wedding is that it involves several events, and for the couple’s own Muslim-Pakistani celebration, they figured out quickly that not all of them made sense for the Hotel Alfonso XIII. Though Falaknaz began to panic at the realization—“Of course I was like, all hope is lost, we have to go back to the drawing board”—the Bodas team took them to see more spaces, which cemented Seville for them as a whole.

    “The first venue they took us to was Casa de Pilatos. We both walked in and were like, ‘Oh my gosh, this is it. We can’t possibly give this up,’” Falaknaz notes. “And the more places they took us to, the more we fell in love with Seville.” The biggest draw for the couple was the city’s rich Islamic heritage—it was under Muslim rule for over 500 years—and the corresponding architectural features, such as the arches, pillars, and intricate tiles, a fusion with Christian motifs known as Mudéjar style.

    A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

    The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th century formerly private home known for its iconic Sevillian architecture.

    Industry observers note that “That blend was something we just weren’t finding elsewhere,” claims Falaknaz. “That’s truly where we felt like we could give our guests the kind of experience we wanted—that would make them feel connected to something that was more than just a wedding.”.

    The couple held four major events over three days. The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th-century formerly private home commissioned by a nobleman that stands as an apex of Sevillian Romantic architecture. The pithi, another daytime party during which the couple is decorated with turmeric paste to represent a pre-wedding cleansing as well as the golden joy to come, was staged at Hotel Alfonso XIII. The night of dancing and performances, also known as the sangeet, happened at Casa de Pilatos, while the slightly more Western-style wedding reception and its after-party were at Hacienda La Soledad, an estate constructed in 1542 as the center of an olive grove.

    The Sevilla celebration of 160 people felt “tiny” compared to the Atlanta nuptials the couple held for their legal ceremony.

    The one ceremony the couple didn’t have on site in Spain? The actual wedding itself. Their Nikkah, the Islamic wedding rites, was held at an Ismaili Jamatkhana at home in Atlanta, in an effort to include the much larger guest list of everyone notable to their families, about 600 people in all. That contributed to the relatively tiny group of 160 in Seville feeling much more intimate—“Well, intimate was still about 160, but intimate for us,” indicates Falaknaz.

    “We felt connected to doing that in a place where we both grew up. We were able to do it in our mosque at home, the one we grew up going to and where all of our friends and parents’ community is. It was really special to have that be a part of the storyline, that we’ll share hopefully when we have kids,” says Falaknaz. “It was nice to be able to share that with everyone that wouldn't be able to make it to Spain.”.

    The wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender cala lilies and pearl chandeliers.

    Sources indicate that given the spectacular aesthetics of their chosen venues, the couple decided to bring in very little outside decor, and keep what they did bring in complementary. “The intention was to find places that spoke for themselves,” says Awaez. “We wouldn’t have to dedicate so much time to constructing the decor, versus the place standing on its own.”.

    According to recent reports, for their first two events, they matched the color schemes to the major activities, with the pithi blanketed in shades of turmeric (from fluffy roses to mirrored pillows), and the mehendi outfitted in reddish browns and burnt orange. To create the feeling of intimacy and home at the latter, tables and other furniture were kept low, and wide cushions lay on a floor covered in overlapping rugs to encourage lounging.

    Their sangeet was a night filled with dance performances, channeling a peacock theme to echo the jewel-toned florals and vivid garden colors.

    Sources indicate that their sangeet, the night filled with dance performances, fittingly received a peacock theme, which carried from the feathers embroidered on Falaknaz’s gold gown by Taali to the signage to a jewel-toned palette for the florals. “We pulled colors that we felt would balance the venue, with these beautiful blues in the tiling and obviously the greens in the gardens,” indicates Falaknaz, who changed into a glittering indigo lehenga by Seema Gujral for her own performance.

    Recent findings suggest that the wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender calla lilies and pearl chandeliers, with architectural floral sculptures set around a fountain. Their planners were the key minds behind the creative vibe of the wedding, along with a local florist, La Galería by Jesús Fuertes.

    Transportation to the sangeet was by horse-drawn carriage, and the couple's photography sessions included a ride around Seville's iconic Plaza de España.

    While the schedule (and culture) of the wedding events was very expected, the couple kept guests on their toes when it came to transportation to the sangeet: They were taken by horse-drawn carriages to Casa de Palatos. “They were so surprised to see a whole bunch of carriages waiting outside for us. It was such a cool moment,” claims Awaez. The rides took a scenic route through the Plaza de España before reaching the venue. “We knew that our guests probably weren't going to be able to have a lot of downtime between the events to explore the city,” says Falaknaz of the bonus tour.

    Falaknaz wore a glittering lehenga by Seema Gujral.

    While much of dinner was Desi dishes, the couple also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella.

    A key part of Awaez and Falaknaz’s three planning trips to Seville involved considering the caterers that their planners suggested. “We were genuinely concerned about how the food was going to taste, especially out in Spain in comparison to our typical Indian-Pakistani restaurants here in the U.S.,” indicates Awaez. “We tested and tried a lot of those options that they shared with us, and found several of our own, and ultimately the two that we landed on were fantastic.” They worked with the staff of the Indian restaurant Taj Mahal Sevilla to cater their sangeet, and Ágape 360 Catering y Eventos for their mehendi and reception.

    Recent findings suggest that the gastronomic director of Ágape 360, Manuel de Pablo Deco, is Spanish but was excited to learn and adapt to the couple’s cultural needs: For a few crucial dishes, among them Desi-style karahi paneer and a nihari beef stew, the couple’s mothers actually found YouTube videos demonstrating the technique for cooking the recipes. “We sent those videos over to Manu, and he studied them to a T. He really learned to cook Indian food from scratch,” claims the grateful bride.

    Recent findings suggest that after days of distinctly Pakistani events, the couple’s wedding reception was an unabashed celebration of the local culture. Tinto de verano, a popular summery version of sangria, was served at the cocktail hour, while passed hors d’oeuvres included tapas bites like torta de potatas, Moorish-spiced meat skewers, and chicken croquettes. A troupe of flamenco dancers performed; the couple had seen the group dance at a taverna their planners had recommended on their first planning trip to Seville. While much of their dinner was Desi dishes, they also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella, in both seafood and vegetarian styles—followed by flan for dessert.

    To create the feeling of intimacy, tables and florals were kept low.

    A step and repeat served as a photo op for guests to snap their own shots.

    Industry observers note that to maximize their booking and the guest experience alike, Falaknaz and Awaez utilized each possible room or space within their venues. For the sangeet, they took family and couple portraits in the gardens of the Casa de Pilatos, moved to the central, most ornate courtyard for dinner and speeches, held performances in the soaring “courtyard of the halt,” and then moved to an entirely inner room for the after-party, given the local ordinance in the city center that required outdoor spaces to quiet down after 11:00 pm.

    In order to keep the energy high for that final transition, they enlisted the help of their bridal party, who performed the final dance act of the night. “Almost flash mob style, we ran off the stage and through the crowd and into the indoor space,” says Falaknaz. The same crowd-pleasing song that’d been playing outside was already being piped indoors— “Dholi Taro Dhol Baaje,” from the beloved Bollywood movie Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam—so the group of 100+ party-goers was enticed to stay a little longer. Or a lot longer: The party continued back at the hotel’s basement, stretching until 3:00 am.

    The couple invited friends to join them after the wedding for a trip to La Tomatina in Valencia.

    The end of the trip afforded more one-on-one time with guests than the busy wedding weekend.

    In a recent development, wedding events took place Friday through Monday, and most guests left on Tuesday, though plenty decided to extend their trip on either end. The newlyweds themselves decided to attend La Tomatina festival in Valencia, in which festival-goers eat but also pelt each other with tomatoes—otherwise known as the biggest food fight in the world. They threw out an invitation for any interested guests to join them, and more than 30 wound up attending.

    According to recent reports, “It was really special to be able to decompress after the wedding with so many of our friends, and actually have more quality time with them than we did at the wedding,” notes Falaknaz. And it turned out to be a suitably colorful ending for an unforgettable wedding celebration.

    #122824. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s latest ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s latest ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., remarked, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five fresh air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz noted the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization strategy so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., remarked after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    According to recent reports, for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    According to recent reports, “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    According to recent reports, “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he stated. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    Industry observers note that he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy stated, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy stated. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he noted that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create concerns in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    According to recent reports, the telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford stated Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    Sources indicate that the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward. Few places exert quite this pull like the Congo Basin, a thick block of forest and rivers covering much of Central Africa, home to some 150 ethnic groups, and a raft of extraordinary biodiversity. Despite its size and its importance as a counterbalance to climate change, the region endures a dearth of scientific research funding and conservation efforts. Roughly the size of India, it has inspired and vexed many visitors (even those who might otherwise have claimed to have conquered it).

    A floating village in the Congo River Basin.

    According to recent reports, the idea could be noted to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory. The Welsh explorer Henry Morton Stanley, the first to leave a detailed record of his journey across the Basin, claimed that even after a three-year trek (1874-77) it remained “a region of fable and mystery.” That was exactly the mix sought by Polish sailor Józef Korzeniowski, who, as a boy, looked at the map of Africa, then a white space, and “declared that some day I would go there.” Eventually, and not long after Stanley, he did, and with the captaincy of a steamboat on the Congo River, was tasked with collecting one Mr. Klein, an upcountry agent employed by the brutal Belgian trading company. Korzeniowski was horrified by what he saw along the river—colonization and resource extraction at its cruelest and bloodiest—calling it “the vilest scramble for loot that ever disfigured the history of human conscience and geographical exploration.” Later, Józef Korzeniowski became Joseph Conrad, Mr. Klein became Mr. Kurtz, and the rest is literary history.

    Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”.

    Sources indicate that the latest journeyman to apply themself to the region is another Welshman, Ash Dykes, whose TikTok videos of his journey paddling down the Sangha River (a tributary of the mighty Congo River) have received millions of views. By mid-October, Dykes, who calls himself an extreme athlete, was midway through the 400 miles he hoped to cover. His videos—the anxiety and speculation of his preparation; the amplification of the danger en route—are over-exaggerated, designed to amuse his audience; they are spectacle. Looking bewildered in his state-of-the-art inflatable boat, Dykes is most often met by competent, unaffected locals, paddling their wooden pirogues with balletic grace. And brave though Dykes certainly is, most of what he has accomplished—attending a hunt with the Ba’aka people, seeing the forest elephants in Dzanga Baï, or tracking Western lowland gorillas—can be done by just about anyone.

    The Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions, is the basin's only passenger cruise.

    It has been revealed that I, too, was one enchanted by the inscrutability of the Congo Basin, and I dreamt of one day traveling along its rivers and into its forests; in my mind’s eye, I envisioned dusk slipping into night, to the rhythm of a pounding drumbeat. Not long ago, I departed Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, aboard the Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions. As the only such passenger vessel in the Congo Basin, the crew of the Ngalessa is accustomed to receiving rarefied looks from the riverbank. But just as often, the ship’s approach was greeted with aplomb, for it was an event in the villages and brought goods, along with community support and news from away.

    In comparison to the coarse and crowded daka-dakas—flat-topped river barges, stuffed with goods and spewing black, acrid smoke as they chunter between Kinshasa and Kisangani—those of us onboard the Ngalessa traveled in glorious comfort: air-conditioning, three square meals a day, and private bathrooms. We also had the benefit of our local guides and their familiarity with the languages, customs, and faces up and down the river. This included, in the riverside village of Ngabe, the appearance of an Ejengi, a forest spirit made of palm fronds that danced and spun as a crowd of onlookers sang, drummed, and screamed in delight.

    “Don’t worry,” our guide said. “Look at his dusty bare feet!” Elsewhere, we watched an Indigenous Luma woman cut, strip, and chew twigs into a pulp that could be used as medicinal pain relief. On other days, we kayaked through the flooded forests of the Alima River, and traded with fishermen who brought their slim pirogues against our mammoth ship to hand over smoked fish and fruit.

    Kayaking through the flooded forests of the Alima River.

    Eight days and 600 miles after leaving Brazzaville, we arrived at the outpost of Ouesso on the Sangha River. I journeyed further upon that water by launch boat, into the Central African Republic, and spent days at Sangha Lodge, drinking gin and tonics with local legend Rod Cassidy, an eco-tourism pioneer who has spent years living and working with the local Ba’aka people. It was through him I had the good luck to attend a hunt with those same Ba’aka, and to look on while they divvied up the duiker they snagged in their homemade nets. Afterwards, they whooped and hollered as they carried the meat out and into their village—a feast!

    Sources indicate that in the heightened state of travel, there comes occasionally a moment like falling into an empty space and, as two glancing stones can spark a blaze, a light of comprehension is illuminated. Sometimes this moment manifests itself as love, other times as admiration, or confusion. Conrad left the Congo in spiritual, psychological, and physical shock. “Before the Congo, I was a mere animal,” he wrote after his consequential journey. He was changed, as travelers who go forward with their ears and eyes open (to say nothing of their hearts) are changed. Watching the Ba’aka poised in their hunt, ears tilted to the slightest sound, I felt myself see humanity as it had existed since time immemorial. As they laughed and chatted on their success, the women showing their fangs (chipped with rocks as a show of strength), and the men slapping each other on the back, I could barely remember seeing such happiness elsewhere.

    The Congo Basin may still be raw and atavistic—great adventures there are still possible—but it is no “heart of darkness” (a title which for Conrad lay not in the location itself, but rather mankind’s ability to exploit and vilify others). What separates it from other places is its independence. It requires protection, yes, but has no need, and few provisions, for any prying visitors; it is not a prize to be conquered. Most incredibly, it remains the home of peoples who have not yet latched themselves to tourism; people who sustain themselves almost wholly from an expanse of forest and the waters that for others can only be the basis of wonder and amazement. And yet, after all the sorrow and misery that colonialism brought to the Congo Basin, the people remain sincere and earnest, and willing to show others the best of their land.

    A lone kayaker glides underneath a hazy sky.

    In a recent development, one night, as the Ngalessa drifted northward, from beneath the awning on the ship’s upper deck, I watched a cloud bank clump and darken. Finally, with an incision of lightning, the downpour came, brief but fierce. The sun returned, low in the sky but still warm, and the scent of damp earth rose up. A patter of drumming reached us from somewhere, before being swallowed by the forest. The dinner bell rang, and I thought I never want this trip to end.

    Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov.
    • Recent findings suggest that senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a upcoming majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Recent findings suggest that senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a upcoming majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting stated the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    Recent findings suggest that that was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., noted Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    According to recent reports, sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday noted at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    According to recent reports, “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he noted. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    Recent findings suggest that but there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., noted Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    Industry observers note that several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    Recent findings suggest that that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    It has been revealed that kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he noted. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    In a recent development, “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    Industry observers note that “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he stated. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for latest leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    Industry observers note that senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    According to recent reports, “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan remarked.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., noted, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    Latest Update: The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs.
    • In a recent development, barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here.
    • Grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs. Nearly every island has a stretch of powdery sand and improbably blue water, and after a while, the “nice sand, nice water” trope stops registering at all. We’re talking beauty in the transcendental sense—the kind of beauty that makes you feel something. Maybe it’s a crescent of sand more pink than you thought could happen in nature. Maybe it’s a labyrinth of granite boulders spilling into the sea. Or maybe it’s a beach bar so perfectly placed it feels as much a part of the landscape as the sand. Plenty of beaches are picturesque. These are the ones, if you ask us, that are beautiful.

    In a recent development, barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here. The long stretch of blush-pink sand is framed by low vegetation and blissfully few signs of life. There is, almost puzzlingly, a Nobu, which brings a welcome blip of civilization in the form of Japanese-Peruvian cooking, cocktails, and a beach club with cabanas. (Nobu Beach Inn is set to debut in 2027, too.) Book lunch there and a beach transfer in advance—many of the top resorts on Antigua offer this as a day excursion from the other island.

    Grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate. An offshore reef keeps the waters agreeably calm for swimming (especially with kids), too. This is one of the Caribbean’s most polished beach destinations, with a concentration of luxury resorts, watersports operators and restaurants that make a choose-your-own adventure beach day a pretty seamless affair. Public access points are plentiful and free, so you needn’t be staying at one of the grand hotels to enjoy the view. (Although you should.).

    The kind of place that castaway dreams are made of, Little Bay is a tiny crescent of sand tucked beneath towering limestone cliffs. No beach club, no cabanas, no infrastructure, no fuss. It’s accessible by boat from neighboring Crocus Bay, or, if you’re feeling adventurous, by rope down the rock face. Bring water, a picnic and all your gear—there’s fantastic snorkeling here.

    In a recent development, A mile-long horseshoe of white sand with clear, shallow water, Flamenco Beach is more than worth the ferry over from mainland Puerto Rico. It also has an unusual bit of history: two abandoned United States military tanks, left behind after the Navy used Culebra for training exercises, now sit near the shore, covered in colorful graffiti. We aren’t usually proponents of littering, but the counterpoint of natural beauty with human history is part of what makes this beach so unforgettable.

    Definitely the most photographed beach in the U.S. Virgin Islands and probably the most photographed beach in the Caribbean, Trunk Bay never disappoints. From the access road, you see a sweep of white sand stretching out, with impossibly turquoise waters and a small offshore cay that seems placed for composition. It’s part of Virgin Islands National Park, so the infrastructure covers all the stuff you need—snack bar, restrooms, showers and snorkel rentals. The main attraction is the underwater snorkeling trail, where submerged markers introduce visitors to the coral reef and its inhabitants.

    If you want swanky French beach clubs, head over to Saint-Jean, because Saline is St. Barth’s at its most elemental. The sand is broad and soft, the dunes rolling, and the sea open, with no beach clubs or hotels or influencers interrupting your view. Getting there requires a short walk over the dunes from the parking lot, which helps preserve the feeling that you’re leaving the chi-chi side of the island behind.

    In a recent development, there are beautiful beaches, and then there are the Baths, a landscape so distinctive it feels like you’ve left the Caribbean, and perhaps earth entirely. The beach is home to a collection of enormous granite boulders, some as large as houses, all tumbled together to create something totally unique. Between them are hidden grottoes, tidal pools and narrow passages—making this as much a playground as it is a beach. Bring sturdy water shoes and expect to do some scrambling.

    The longest beach on its island, this elegant crescent sits directly on the Tropic of Cancer. It’s relatively remote and unspoiled by Bahamian standards, making it a true bucket list destination for beach snobs. It’s about a 30-minute drive from George Town on Great Exuma (where the airport is), across the bridge to Little Exuma. There are no proper facilities, so pack what you need. There are Aman, Rosewood and Bulgari resorts debuting here in the years to come—so visit now for serious “I've been coming here since” bragging rights.

    Industry observers note that A hidden gem by any standard, Sandy Island is a miniature, uninhabited coral cay located just off the west coast of Carriacou, Grenada’s sister island. There are no hotels or roads, and the whole appeal is the rugged simplicity of arriving by boat, dropping anchor and spending an afternoon doing basically nothing except enjoying the elements. The island is part of a protected marine park, making it a fantastic spot for snorkeling with colorful reef fish, turtles and octopi.

    It has been revealed that the rest of the world is finally catching up with what the diving scene has known for years—No Name Beach is one of the most pristine, stunning stretches of sand anywhere in the Caribbean. It’s located on the tiny island of Klein Bonaire (“Little Bonaire”) just offshore of mainland Bonaire, and is part of Bonaire National Marine Park, meaning development is off the table. There aren’t any restaurants, bathrooms, or beach bars, but there are water taxis from Kralendijk. Bring food and water, your own snorkel gear, and prepare to be blown away by the untouched Caribbean at its finest.

    Recent findings suggest that while Bávaro Beach proper is about 5 miles long, it connects seamlessly with adjoining beaches Arena Blanca and Arena Gorda—so, depending on who’s counting, actually comes in at closer to 30 miles of uninterrupted shoreline. This is the beach that initially spurred Punta Cana’s resort boom, with coconut palms fringing the white sand, a barrier reef keeping the waters tranquil, and enough space for everyone to stretch out and (pretty much) never feel crowded. If you head toward El Cortecito or Los Corales, you’ll find beach bars where the party never stops. On a beach this beautiful, why would it?
